source_title: GE aviation and energy businesses start trading on NYSE, marking the end of the conglomerate
publisher_issuer: CNBC; corroborated by GE Vernova press releases and GE SEC 8-K filings (CIK 0000040545)
company_context: General Electric, a 130-year-old industrial conglomerate, entered severe distress in the late 2010s under heavy debt and weak power/capital businesses. New CEO Larry Culp (2018) cut the dividend to a penny, aggressively reduced debt, and ultimately broke the company into three public companies, completing the split on April 2, 2024 (GE Aerospace, GE Vernova, GE HealthCare spun off January 2023).
macro_context: Post-2017 industrial downturn, GE Capital legacy liabilities, power-market weakness; later strong aerospace recovery and energy-transition demand benefiting the separated entities.
evidence_summary: Facing crisis, GE under Larry Culp slashed its 119-year-old dividend to one cent per share starting 2019 and pursued large-scale debt reduction, targeting more than $75 billion of gross debt reduction from end-2018 through 2021 (including ~$30 billion via the AerCap transaction). The conglomerate was dismantled into three companies: GE HealthCare (spun off January 3, 2023) and GE Aerospace and GE Vernova (April 2, 2024). The outcome was mixed/partial: shareholders who held through the crisis suffered massive value destruction earlier, but the surviving entities (notably GE Aerospace and GE Vernova) recovered strongly post-split.
owner_decision_context: CEO Larry Culp decided to deleverage aggressively (cutting the dividend, selling assets) and ultimately to abandon the conglomerate structure, separating into focused public companies to restore value.
action_taken: Cut the dividend to one cent, reduced gross debt by more than $75 billion, and broke the conglomerate into three independent public companies (HealthCare 2023; Aerospace and Vernova 2024).
outcome_evidence: Completion of the three-way split, >$75 billion debt reduction, and strong post-split performance of GE Aerospace and GE Vernova confirm a partial/mixed recovery: severe earlier value destruction followed by restructuring-driven stabilization and recovery.
source_limitations: WebFetch of cnbc.com and sec.gov returned HTTP 403; figures confirmed across CNBC, CNN, Motley Fool, GE Vernova press releases, and GE SEC 8-K snippets (CIK 0000040545). The '$134 billion' total-debt framing was not corroborated and is omitted; debt-reduction figures are cited as company-stated targets/achievements.
directly_stated: GE cut its 119-year-old dividend to one cent per share starting 2019 (announced Oct 30, 2018)
GE targeted/achieved more than $75 billion gross debt reduction from end-2018 to 2021 (~$30B via AerCap)
Breakup announced Nov 9, 2021; GE HealthCare spun off Jan 3, 2023; Aerospace and Vernova split April 2, 2024
inferred: The deleveraging and breakup constituted a strategic correction that stabilized the surviving businesses (partial recovery)
Earlier shareholders bore heavy losses, making the multi-year outcome mixed rather than a clean turnaround
why_useful_for_opsiq: Outcome-5 mixed case: severe debt/solvency distress addressed via deleveraging and conglomerate breakup, yielding partial recovery. Tests whether the engine evaluates multi-year restructuring as a mixed outcome and links debt-solvency pressure to the corrective strategic actions.
